hypothesis: The neuron responds selectively to high-contrast, elongated parallel bands or ridges, typically characterized by alternating stripes of bright luminosity and deep shadow. These features frequently manifest as sharp specular highlights on cylindrical metallic surfaces (such as pens, harmonicas, or pipes) or as layered geometric stratifications (such as industrial grooves or concentric curved bands). The neuron is invariant to object identity, material context, and precise orientation, responding robustly to both diagonal and horizontal arrangements as long as the strict linear organization and stark luminosity contrast are preserved. The activating features are predominantly achromatic, consisting of bright white, silver, or light grey strips set against deep black or dark charcoal backgrounds. Spatially, these linear structures usually traverse the frame diagonally or horizontally, typically occupying 30–80% of the image area and dominating the composition with their directional flow.
